title: Stalin's spy in Tokyo hanged

facts.text: On 7 November 1944, Japan hanged the Soviet spy Richard Sorge at Sugamo Prison in Tokyo; the trap fell at 10:20 a.m.
His Japanese collaborator Hotsumi Ozaki, a journalist and former adviser to Prime Minister Fumimaro Konoe, was hanged at Sugamo earlier the same day.
The date was the anniversary of the Russian Revolution.
Sorge worked in Tokyo from 1933 under cover as a German journalist for the Frankfurter Zeitung, and he was a member of the Nazi Party.
He became a close friend of the German ambassador, Eugen Ott, and by the time of his arrest he had an office inside the German embassy, where he saw secret documents and cables.
In May and June 1941 he warned Moscow that Germany was about to attack the Soviet Union, but Stalin ignored the warnings.
In autumn 1941 he reported that Japan would not attack the Soviet Union that year and would strike south instead.
Stalin then moved troops from Siberia to defend Moscow, but historians debate how much his decision rested on Sorge, since Soviet codebreakers were also reading Japanese messages.
Japanese police arrested Sorge in Tokyo on 18 October 1941, days after Ozaki was taken.
Japan's investigation of the spy ring led to 35 arrests.
In November 1964, twenty years after his death, the Soviet Union named Sorge a Hero of the Soviet Union.
